## Guided reading

Read sections **1.2**, **1.5**, and **1.8** closely, and skim the rest. Keep
these questions in mind as you read: the answers are all in the text, and the
problems below check the same ideas.

**1.2 History's hockey stick**

  b. Why does the book insist on GDP *per capita* rather than GDP?
  c. What are international dollars, and what problem do they solve?

## History's hockey stick

*The first two charts, and Activity 1 on your worksheet.*

**1.** For most of the last thousand years, GDP per capita was roughly flat
everywhere. Then it began to rise.

  a. Roughly when did sustained growth begin in Britain?
  b. Did every country's take-off happen at the same time? Order the five
     countries on the chart from earliest to latest.
  c. What does the flat part of the chart tell you about how a person's living
     standard compared with their grandparents'?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. Around 1800. Growth is visible from about 1700 and unmistakable after 1800.

b. No. Britain first, then the US during the 1800s, then Mexico, China, and
   India, whose lines only turn upward in the second half of the twentieth
   century.

c. It was about the same. Living standards moved up and down with harvests,
   disease, and war, but there was no sustained improvement from one
   generation to the next.

</details>

**2.** On the chart we looked at, GDP per capita in 2022 was about \$56,000 in
the US and about \$7,800 in India.

  a. Roughly how many times higher was the US figure?
  b. In 1800 the two were much closer together. What happened in between to
     open the gap?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. About $56{,}000 \div 7{,}800 \approx 7$ times.

b. Britain and then the US began sustained growth around 1800 and kept
   growing for two centuries. India's take-off did not come until after 1950.
   The gap is the result of starting at different times, not of one country
   falling behind from a high level.

</details>

## Measuring prosperity

*The GDP per capita slide.*

**3.** Explain in one or two sentences:

  a. What does GDP measure?
  b. Why do we divide it by population before comparing countries?
  c. Why is GDP per capita only a proxy for living standards, not the same
     thing?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. GDP is a country's output: everything it produces in a year, valued at
   market prices. That total is also everyone's total income.

b. A larger country has a higher GDP simply because it has more people.
   Dividing by population gives the average person's income, which is what we
   want to compare.

c. It is an average, so it says nothing about how income is shared out, and it
   leaves out things people care about that are never bought or sold.

</details>

**4.** A haircut costs 300 pesos in Mexico City and \$30 in Los Angeles. The
market exchange rate is 20 pesos per dollar.

  a. Converted at the exchange rate, what does the Mexico City haircut cost in
     dollars?
  b. Both haircuts are the same service. What does your answer to (a) tell you
     about converting Mexican incomes at the exchange rate?
  c. What do economists do instead, and what are the resulting units called?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. $300 \div 20 = \$15$.

b. The exchange rate makes the Mexican haircut look like half the service,
   when it is the same haircut. Converting incomes this way understates what a
   peso actually buys, so Mexico looks poorer than it is.

c. They convert at *purchasing power parity* (PPP) rates, chosen so that \$20
   buys in any country what \$20 buys in the US. Incomes converted this way are
   measured in *international dollars*.

</details>

## Adam Smith

*The founding question, and the Adam Smith slide.*

**5.** Smith asked how millions of strangers, none of them in charge, end up
supplying each other with what they need.

  a. What name did he give his answer?
  b. He wrote: "It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or
     the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own
     interest." Put that sentence in your own words.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. The *invisible hand*: markets coordinate the decisions of millions of
   people with no one planning the result.

b. The butcher sells you dinner because it is in their own interest to do so,
   not because they care about you. Self-interested behavior, channeled through
   markets, ends up serving other people.

</details>

**6.** Smith argued that prosperity came from the division of labor, and that
the division of labor is limited by the extent of the market.

  a. What is the *division of labor*?
  b. In his pin factory, ten workers each doing one or two of eighteen steps
     made close to 50,000 pins a day. How many could each make working alone?
  c. What does "limited by the *extent of the market*" mean? Why could a
     village not support the pin factory?
  d. Name one thing that widened the market in Smith's time.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. Instead of each worker making a whole product, each specializes in one step
   of the process.

b. Barely one pin a day each. Specializing raised output by a factor of
   thousands.

c. Specialization only pays if the output can be sold. A village could not buy
   50,000 pins a day, so a pin-maker there would have to make whole pins, and
   other things besides, rather than specialize.

d. Canals, better roads, or foreign trade. And the prosperity that followed
   widened the market further.

</details>

## Technology

*The technological revolution, and the technology slide.*

**7.** In economics, "technology" means more than machines.

  a. Give the economic definition of a technology.
  b. Which of these is technological progress? Explain each.
     (i) A bakery buys a second oven and bakes twice as many cakes.
     (ii) A bakery finds a recipe that bakes the same cake with less flour and
     in half the time.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. A technology is a process that takes a set of materials and other inputs,
   including the work of people and machines, and creates an output. A cake
   recipe is a technology.

b. Only (ii). Technological progress reduces the inputs needed to produce a
   given output. In (i) the bakery produces more, but it uses proportionally
   more inputs to do it, so the technology itself has not changed. In (ii) the
   same cake takes less flour and less time.

</details>

## Capitalism

*From the capitalist revolution through the three institutions, and Activity 2
on your worksheet.*

**8.** Define each term, and say how the three relate to one another.

  a. Economic system
  b. Institutions
  c. Capitalism

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. A way of organizing the economy that is distinctive in its basic
   institutions.

b. The laws and informal rules that regulate social interactions among people,
   and between people and the biosphere. The rules of the game.

c. An economic system characterized by a particular combination of
   institutions: private property, markets, and firms.

So: institutions are the rules; an economic system is a way of organizing the
economy defined by which rules it has; capitalism is the particular system
built on those three.

</details>

**9.** Which of the three institutions are present in each case?

  a. A family farm that grows food only for itself.
  b. A Saturday farmers' market where growers sell their own produce.
  c. A state-owned steel mill in East Germany in 1970.
  d. A ride-sharing company with 1,000 drivers.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. Private property only. The family owns the farm, but nothing is bought or
   sold and no one is hired.

b. Private property and markets. Growers own what they sell and exchange
   voluntarily, but each works for themselves rather than for a firm.

c. Neither private property in capital goods nor firms in the capitalist
   sense: the state owned the mill and output was set by a plan rather than by
   an owner seeking profit.

d. All three. The company owns capital, hires and directs drivers, and sells
   rides on a market for profit.

</details>

**10.** Can a market work without private property? Can a firm exist without
markets? Which institution has to be in place for the others to work, and why?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Private property comes first. Exchange means transferring the right to use
something, so if no one has the right to exclude others from a good or to
transfer it, there is nothing to sell. A firm needs both: it must own its
capital goods, and it must be able to sell its output on a market to make a
profit.

</details>

## Did capitalism cause the take-off?

*The causation slide, the two Germanies, and "why not everywhere?"*

**11.** Capitalism spread and living standards rose at about the same time.

  a. Why is that alone not enough to conclude that capitalism caused the rise?
  b. What is a natural experiment?
  c. Why is East versus West Germany after 1945 more convincing evidence than
     comparing the US with India?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. Correlation is not causation. Something else could have caused both, or the
   causation could run the other way, with rising living standards making
   capitalist institutions more likely to spread.

b. A situation in which similar people or places end up under different
   conditions for reasons unrelated to the outcome being studied, so the
   outcomes can be compared as if in an experiment.

c. In 1950 the two Germanies had the same people, language, history, and
   roughly the same income, and were then divided into a capitalist West and a
   centrally planned East. Almost everything except the economic system was
   held constant. The US and India differ in countless other ways, so a
   comparison between them cannot isolate the effect of any one of them.

</details>

**12.** Most countries today are capitalist, yet living standards differ
enormously. Give two reasons why.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Any two of:

- **Colonialism.** In India, living standards did not rise substantially until
  well after independence from British rule. In much of Latin America,
  independence in the early nineteenth century did not change economic
  fortunes.
- **Institutions and politics.** Capitalism is not one thing. Private property,
  markets, or firms may fail or be poorly protected, and governments differ in
  how well they regulate them.
- **Public goods.** Governments also provide infrastructure, education, and the
  rule of law, and countries differ greatly in how well they do this.

</details>

## The other hockey stick

*Emissions, temperature, and the biosphere.*

**13.** World carbon emissions have the same shape as the GDP chart: flat, then
a steep rise.

  a. Why do the two charts look alike?
  b. The economy is drawn inside society, which is drawn inside the biosphere.
     What does the economy take from the biosphere, and what does it send back?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

a. The technologies behind the take-off worked by burning carbon: coal for
   steam engines and factories, then oil and gas. Producing more meant burning
   more, so output and emissions rose together.

b. It takes energy, materials, and food, and it returns waste, emissions, and
   heat. The economy is not a closed loop: everything it makes starts as
   something taken from the biosphere and ends as something returned to it.

</details>

**14.** Write down the definition of economics we ended on, and say which two
kinds of interaction it covers.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Economics is the study of how people interact with each other and with their
natural environment in producing their livelihoods, and how this changes over
time and differs across societies.

The two interactions are between people (buying, selling, working, and the
institutions that govern all of it) and between people and nature (what
production takes from the biosphere and returns to it).

</details>
